text: September 11, 1913. Mr. James D. Scott may be reinstated in the Railway Mail Service, without regard to the length of time he has been out of the service. The Postmaster General reports that he was appointed a railway mail clerk on October 17, 1900, at $800 per annum, and promoted through the successive grades until he received a salary of $1,100 per annum; that he resigned voluntarily, April 17,1911; that his record as a clerk is good, and his reinstatement would be to the benefit of the service. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending that an Executive order be issued in this case.

Watkins may be transferred from the nonapportioned to the appor- tioned service of the Treasury Department, and promoted to the position of clerk, with- out civil-service rules. This order 1s recommended by the Secretary of the Treasury in view of the fact that Mrs. Ryon was before marriage an efficient employee. March 21, 1917. Mr. William J. Martin may be appointed to a competitive position in the Treasury Department. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, who states that Mr. Martin has rendered very efficient service for several years in an ex- cepted position as executive clerk, has made an excellent record, has a grasp of the many details and difficult problems connected with the work of the office, has become eculiarly familiar with the personnel and appointments under the internal revenue ws, and that the action proposed is desired in order to permit the extension of Mr. Martin’s activities. For the reasons stated by the Secretary the Civil Service Commission concurs in the recommendation.

August 8, 1916. The year limit on eligibility for reinstatement is hereby waived to permit the reinstatement of Mr, Arthur 8. Hull as a fourth assistant examiner in the Patent Office. In view of Mr. Hull's efficient service as an examiner and his experience acquired during a service of four and one-half years, and in view of the continuing difficulty of obtaining a sufficient number of qualified eligibles to meet the demands of the Patent Office for examiners, the Secretary of the Interior recommends this order and the Civil Service Commission concurs in the recommendation.

March 29, 1916. Mr. Charles H. Slack may be reinstated to the position of compositor at 50 cents per hour in the Government Printing Office without reference to the period of his separation from the service. Mr. Slack was appointed in the Government Printing Office December 3, 1901, and resigned September 23, 1904. A certificate was requested for his reinstatement within the year of his eligi- bility and was issued by this office, but it was returned unused by the Public Printer February 27, 1906. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Public Printer with the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission because of Mr. Slack’s efficiency while in the service, and because of the fact that since leaving the service he has been continuously engaged in work that would maintain and add to that efficiency.

Herndon may be appointed to a clerkship in the Bureau of the Census, Department of Commerce, at $1,000 per annum, without reference to the requirement of examination under the civil-service rules. Mr. Herndon was appointed a clerk at $900 per annum in the Bureau of the Census on June 1, 1900; promoted to $1,000 September 1, 1900; and to $1,200 November 15, 1901. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of War and the Chief of Engineers, with the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission. January 20, 1015. Mr. Newton C. Llewellyn maybe reinstated as a carrier in the Knoxville, Tenn., post office without regard to the length of his separation from the service. Mr. Llewellyn entered the Postal Service as a substitute carrier at Knoxville on January 18, 1895, and remained in the service until February 28, 1907, when he resigned. The Postmaster General states that Mr. Llewellyn's record is good, that it is a meritorious case, and that the department has no objection to the issuance of an order.

May 6, 1914. Mr. James D. Troy may be promoted from the position of assistant engineer on the statutory roll of the Secretary of Agriculture, at a salary of $1,000 per annum, to the position, of assistant chief engineer on the same roll, at a salary of $1,400 per annum, without reference to civil-service Rule XI, clause (b) of section 2. The Secretary of Agriculture recommends the promotion of Mr. Troy, who has been in the department since July, 1908, for the reason that he has served continuously in the power house and has been familiar with the plant for years and knows it in ever detail. He regards the thorough practical qualifications of Mr. Troy to be of muc value to the department and believes it to be in the interest of efficient and econom- ical service to promote him to the position in question. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation.

September 14, 1915. James O. Brockenshire, chief musician, United States Army, retired, may be appointed as inspector of musical instruments at $780 per annum, Quartermaster Corps of the Army, without examination under the civil-service rules. The Acting Secretary of War states that the waiving of the civil-service rules to authorize the appointment of Mr. Brockenshire is requested by the Acting Quarter- master General of the Army, in view of his long service in the Army as chief musician and his varied experience with Army bands, which especially qualify him for the position. The Acting Quartermaster General reports that he is a thorough musician, able to play almost any instrument in Army bands, and is just the type of inspector needed by the depot quartermaster at Philadelphia, under whom he has been em- ployed at different times during the past two years, rendering entirely satisfactory service. .Mr. Brockenshire was in the military service as musician for nearly thirty years, voluntarily retiring on June 1, 1914, with a “most excellent character.” During his service, with the exception of about one year, he was with the Seventh Cavalry. The acting adjutant of the Seventh Cavalry states that he had been held in the highest esteem by every officer and enlisted man with whom he had come in contact officially and personally and was universally admired and respected both as a soldier and as a man because of his constant devotion to duty and courteous treatment of his associates. Maj. Gen. J. F. Bell, who knew him about 30 years, states that he is one of the best men he had ever known, being entirely sober, reliable, upright, and honorable, always courteous and most obliging, because he is a gentleman at heart; and, further, that he is a disciplinarian with a special faculty for getting along with and managing bands. Almost if not equally strong testimonials were given by ins. Gen. Garling- ton, Brig. Gen. Charles Morton, Brig. Gen. T. N. Baldwin, retired, and numerous officers of the Seventh Cavalry. Because of Mr. Brockenshire’s unusual service, splendid character, and musical ability, so strongly stated by Army officers who have known him intimately, and his demonstrated qualifications for the position of inspector of musical instruments, the Civil Service Commission recommends this order.

August 6, 1915. Mr. Francis J. Reinhard, of Indiana, may be appointed to the position of law clerk in the office of the Solicitor of the Treasury, without reference to the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Attorney General, who states that the relationship existing between the solicitor and the man holding this position is quite confidential; that the duties of the office require a man of considerable expe- rience as a lawyer; that Solicitor Becker of the Treasury, who personally knows Mr. Reinhard, is familiar with his qualifications, has confidence in him, and has recom- mended that he be appointed, and that an effort has been made to find some one within the civil service possessing the special qualifications needed, but without success. The Attorney General further states that he believes the interests of the public service would be subserved by exempting the appointment.

December 20, 1916. Mr. William C. Rader may be appointed Assistant to the Director of the Bureau of War Risk Insurance in the Treasury Department without compliance with civil-service rules. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, who states that the position of Assistant to the Director of the Bureau of War Risk Insurance is a technical one; that there is no person.in the Treasury Department qualified to fill the position, and that Mr. Rader possesses the necessary qualifications, and that his appointment will be in the interest of the service. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation.

May 9, 1917. Mr. Horace M. Albright may be appointed as Assistant Director of the National - Park Service. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Interior who states that Mr. Albright, as assistant attorney of the department, has been assisting in the management of the national park system for several years; that he is very familiar with the administration of the parks and with their problems; that he is personally acquainted with the field force and with the park concessioners who are under contract with the department to provide hotel accommodations and transporta- tion service for the comfort and convenience of the traveling public; that he knows the conditions under which these concessioners operate, and has drafted the contracts under which several of the larger concessions are conducted; that he understands thoroughly the policies that have been adopted for the development and promotion of the national park system; that he is concerned with the preparation of legislation relating to the national parks, reports to Congress on national park legislation, and is charged with the duty of defending departmental estimates for appropriations for the park system. The Secretary also states that it is necessary that the Assistant Director of the National Park Service be acquainted with the parks and their problems at the time he assumes his office; that he be a lawyer in order that he may give consideration to all legal matters relating to the National Park Service, and that Mr. Albright possesses these qualifications. The Civil Service Commission concurs in the recommendation for the issuance of this order.

February 5, 1914. Mr. Howard L. Strawn may be reinstated to an appropriate position in the competi- tive service in the Government Printing Office. Mr. Strawn served almost continuously as a clerk from July 14, 1890, to July 1, 1895, and as an inspector from July 1, 1895, to July 1, 1909, when his designation was changed to inspector of paper and material. On June 30, 1911, he was dropped from the rolls of the Government Printing Office because of a legislative provision that the salary of the inspector for the Joint Committee on Printing should be paid one half by the Secre- tary of the Senate and the other half by the Clerk of the House of Representatives. From July 1, 1911, to October 15, 1913, he served as inspector of paper and material for the Joint Committee on Printing, his services being terminated on the latter date. In view of the long and efficient service of Mr. Strawn in the Government Printing Office, both before and after the classification of that service, and his subsequent service under the Joint Committee on Printing, the commission concurs in recommend- ing an order permitting his reinstatement in the competitive classified service.

Mrs. Ida K. Marsh may be employed for one year in an appropriate position in the Bureau of the Census, without regard to the civil service rules. Mrs. Marsh is the widow of Raymond C. Marsh, who served in the United States Army from May 18, 1918, to July 25, 1919, and died on April 20, 1928. He left his family without means of support, and Mrs. Marsh has had to place her two children in an orphanage. She has served in temporary Government positions for an aggregate of about three years but has no eligibility for reinstatement. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of Commerce, and with the restriction that it does not confer upon Mrs. Marsh any status for subsequent employment in the classified service. HERBERT HOOVER The White House, April 25, 1930. Mrs. Marsh served as a clerk in the Treasury Department from 1896 to 1903.

October 1, 1913. Mrs. Mary D. Hanna may be appointed to a clerkship in the classified service subject to such tests of fitness as the Civil Service Commission may require. Mrs. Hanna is the widow of Capt. Guy B. G. Hanna, Coast Artillery, who met his death while in the line of duty, by the premature explosion of a service charge during night target practice. In view of the tragic circumstances of the case and the fact that it 18 now necessary for Mrs. Hanna to earn her own livelihood the Secretary of War recommended the issuance of an Executive order waiving the requirement of exami- nation under the civil-service rules to permit her appointment. The Civil Service Commission recommended that the appointment be permitted, subject to appropriate tests of fitness,

May 21, 1920. Mrs. Margaret H. Bowen may be appointed to a position in the Postal Service without regard to the requirements of the civil-service rules and regulations. Mrs. Bowen was temporarily employed in the Washington City post office during the period of the late war and performed satisfactory service. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Postmaster General. Her late husband was appointed a letter carrier on May 12, 1890.

December 5, 1913. Miss Eva L. Moran may be appointed to a clerkship in the War Department without reference to the requirement of examination under the civil-service rules. Miss Moran is the daughter of Thomas M. Moran, who has served as a clerk in the War Department for 50 years and whose service during all that time has been faithful and meritorious. He has now reached an advanced age, is seriously ill, and it is reported that it is likely he will never be able to return to duty. The Secretary of War recommends that an order be issued authorizing the appoint- ment of Miss Moran. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recom- mendation of the Secretary of War.
